My husband asked me last Thursday if I'd eaten dinner. I said yes. I hadn't. I have been lying to the man I've been married to for 38 years about food, about the bathroom, about how I feel, ever since the shot started working. The weight is coming off. So is the woman he married.

I am 61 years old. I have been on Mounjaro for 14 months. I have lost 52 pounds. I have a husband, two daughters, four grandchildren, and a kitchen table where I have been telling my first real lies in 38 years of marriage.

I'd like to back up.

I went on Mounjaro in February of last year for the same reason every woman in my book club went on it. I had spent 4 decades trying to lose the same 50 pounds. I had done Weight Watchers in the 80s. I had done Atkins in the 90s. I had done Whole30 in 2014 and a juice cleanse in 2017 and Noom in 2020 and the carnivore diet for one miserable summer in 2022.

By the time my doctor mentioned Mounjaro to me at my annual physical, I had stopped believing my body was capable of losing weight at all. I had decided I was just going to be the size I was, and I was going to learn to be okay with it, and I was going to die in a body that had never felt like mine.

The shot changed that in 6 weeks.

I lost 11 pounds the first month. The food noise that had been the soundtrack of my entire adult life went quiet. I stopped thinking about my next meal during my current meal. I stopped opening the refrigerator at 9pm just to look. I cried in my car at the Whole Foods parking lot the first time I left a restaurant having not finished my plate, because I had not done that since I was a teenager.

The shot did exactly what they said it would do.

I bought clothes I had not been able to wear in 12 years. My husband told me at the bathroom mirror one Saturday morning that he could see the woman he married coming back. I cried again. I have cried more in the last 14 months than I cried in the previous 30 years.

The shot also did something else.

The shot started slowing my stomach down.

The first month I noticed I was bloated by dinner. I thought it was the carbonated water. I switched to flat. The bloat stayed.

Month two I noticed I was going to the bathroom every other day instead of every day. I drank more water. Nothing happened.

Month three the burps started. The sulfur ones. The kind that taste like rotten eggs and come up without warning at the worst possible moment. I had one come up while I was reading to my granddaughter on my lap. I excused myself to the kitchen and I cried at the sink because I was 60 years old and I could not control what was coming out of my own mouth.

That was the first lie.

She asked me where Grandma went and I told her I had to check on the cookies. There were no cookies. There has not been a baked good in my house since the shot took the want for them away.

The lying started small. It always does.

By month five I was telling my husband I had eaten lunch when I had not, because the brick in my stomach from the lunch I had skipped two days ago would not let anything new in. By month seven I was telling my book club I had read the chapter when I had not, because I had been sitting in the recliner at 3am for the third night in a row trying to relieve the pressure under my ribs and I had not opened a book in 6 weeks. By month ten I was telling my daughter on the phone that my husband and I had gone out to dinner Friday night when actually I had told him I had a migraine and we had stayed home, because going out meant a 90 minute window in a restaurant and a 20 minute drive home and there was no version of that where the bloat or the burps or the brick did not show up at the table.

The lies got bigger because the truth got harder to say out loud.

The truth was that I was losing 50 pounds and I was also losing the ability to be in a room with the people I loved.

The truth was that I had a husband who was waking up every morning to a smaller wife and going to bed every night to a stranger who would not let him hold her because she was too bloated to be touched.

The truth was that I had been buying constipation products at three different stores so the cashiers would stop recognizing me.

The truth was that I had a bathroom shelf with $1,400 worth of Miralax and Metamucil and magnesium and senna and probiotics and prune juice and Smooth Move tea and a fiber gummy I had bought because the woman at GNC told me her sister-in-law swore by it.

The truth was that not one of those products had given me a single normal week of bathroom mornings in 11 months.

The truth was that I was a 61 year old woman who had spent 4 decades wishing she was thinner and now that she finally was, she had become a person who could not eat dinner with her own husband.

I sat at my kitchen table on a Tuesday afternoon in October and I tried to remember the last time I had told my husband the truth about how I was feeling. I could not.

I called my older daughter that night and I cried into the phone for 20 minutes and I told her about the lies. About the dinners I had skipped. About the chapters I had not read. About the night I had pretended to be asleep when my husband came to bed because I could not face the conversation about why I was not letting him near me.

She was very quiet on the other end of the line. Then she said, "Mom, I think this is the shot. I think you are not depressed. I think your body is in trouble and you have been carrying it alone."

That sentence cracked something open.

I had been carrying it alone. For 14 months. Because the shame of admitting that the medication that had given me back my body had also taken away my ability to sit at a dinner table was bigger than the shame of lying to my own husband.

She sent me a video the next morning.

It was a gastroenterologist on Instagram talking about something I had never heard a doctor say before. She said GLP-1 medication does not slow your colon. It slows your stomach. By up to 70% in some patients. She said the food sits there fermenting, which is where the sulfur burps come from. She said the bloat is at the upper belly because the food is stalled at the upper belly.

And she said every laxative on every shelf at every drugstore in America is designed to work on the colon. The colon is six feet downstream of the stomach.

She said women like me have been treating the wrong organ.

I watched the video three times.

I made my husband come into the kitchen and I made him watch it.

He sat with me at the table. He looked at the bathroom shelf full of bottles he had been pretending not to see for 11 months. He looked at me. And he said, "you have been pointing at the wrong room."

That is the sentence the doctor used in the video. He had not heard it from her. He had figured it out from 14 months of watching me lie to him at the dinner table.

I asked him why he had not said anything.

He said, "Because every time I asked, you told me you were fine. And I knew if I pushed, I would lose you faster."

I have been married to him for 38 years. I do not think I have ever been more ashamed and more grateful in the same minute as I was at my kitchen table that Tuesday afternoon.

I want you to picture your stomach as a kitchen sink.

Not a colon. Not "your gut." A kitchen sink with a drain at the bottom that empties into the rest of the plumbing.

When the drain works, you can rinse anything down. Coffee grounds, last night's pasta water, the scraps off the dinner plates. It all goes down. The sink stays clean.

GLP-1 medication does one thing extraordinarily well. It half-clogs the drain.

That is in fact the point of the medication. It slows your stomach so food sits there longer and you feel full longer and you eat less. The slowdown is the medication doing its job. That is why the shot works.

But here is what nobody told me at month one.

For about 79% of women over 50 on a GLP-1 longer than 12 months, that drain doesn't just slow. It half-clogs and stays half-clogged.

Picture a sink with a half-clogged drain.

The water doesn't go down. It pools.

You scrape another plate into the sink. The food bits don't rinse. They float.

You scrape a second plate. A third. The pile builds.

The pile sits in standing water and starts to ferment. Anyone who has left dishes in a clogged sink for 48 hours in summer knows that smell. That sulfur. That rotten egg note.

That smell, coming up through the drain into the kitchen, is the same smell that crawled up my esophagus while I was reading to my granddaughter.

The sulfur burps. The brick under my ribs. The bloat. The Sunday lunch still sitting there Wednesday. The lies at the dinner table.

It is all the same thing.

It is a kitchen sink with a half-clogged drain.

The villain has a name. It is the slowed stomach.

And every single thing on my bathroom shelf, the Miralax, the Metamucil, the magnesium, the prune juice, the senna, the probiotics, every single one of them was pointed at my colon.

The colon is six feet under the floor on the other side of the house.

The clog is in the sink.

Pouring drain cleaner into the bathtub does nothing for a clog in the kitchen sink.

That, in one sentence, is why I had been lying to my husband for 11 months.

Not because my body was broken. Not because I was a difficult case. Not because I had "Mounjaro gut."

Because every product I had reached for had been treating the wrong room. And the only way to keep reaching for it without admitting the truth was to lie about how much it was costing me.

But here is what most women on the shot don't believe me when I tell them.

The slowed stomach is not a mystery. It is not a permanent broken thing. It is a mechanical problem with a mechanical fix.

There are three plant compounds with research behind them that work upstream, at the stomach, where the medication has actually slowed things down.

Three compounds my doctor never mentioned. Three compounds the woman at the pharmacy never mentioned. Three compounds that are not in a single bottle on the laxative aisle of any store I had been buying from for 11 months.

The first one is called apigenin. It is a flavonoid concentrated in celery juice extract and chamomile. The research on it goes back decades. Apigenin works on the smooth muscle in the stomach wall. It helps the stomach remember how to contract on its own. It does not override the medication. It does not force urgency the way a laxative does. It works at the on-ramp, where the slowdown is, instead of the off-ramp where the laxatives have been firing.

The second is chlorophyllin. The stabilized form of the green pigment in plants. It binds the sulfur compounds and methane your gut bacteria are producing while the food sits there fermenting. It does not mask the smell. It deactivates the molecules the smell is made of.

The third is a soluble prebiotic fiber. Completely different from the bulking psyllium fiber the pharmacy keeps pushing on women like me. Bulking fiber adds mass to a stomach that cannot move what is already there. Soluble prebiotic fiber softens the food bolus while it is still in the stomach so the contractions, when they come back, have something soft to push.

Wake the stomach. Clear the ferment. Move the chain.

All three aiming at the upstream organ. None of them at the colon.

Six feet up from where the laxatives have been pointing for 11 months.

That is why I take Motilli.

It is the only product I have found that has all three compounds in the doses the research called for.

I want to be very honest about this because I do not want anyone reading this thinking I am sponsored or that I get paid every time someone clicks something. I have told my story so many times in the last 6 weeks at book club, at my hairdresser, at the grocery checkout, that my daughter said I should write it all down so I could just send it to people.

Motilli is a small company. They make a heart-shaped gummy. Two a day.

Apigenin from standardized celery extract, not powder, because powder loses the active compound on the shelf. Chlorophyllin in the stabilized form. A soluble prebiotic fiber, not psyllium, not bulk filler.

Most apigenin products on the shelf use ground-up celery powder at one-twentieth of the dose the studies used. Most chlorophyll products are sold for body odor. Most fiber products stack soluble fiber on top of psyllium and call it gut support.

Motilli does not. That is the whole reason it works.

I started the gummies on a Monday morning. By Friday morning of that first week the sulfur burps stopped. Just stopped. I had not gone 4 days without one in 11 months.

That Friday night my husband and I went out to dinner for the first time in 6 weeks. I did not lie about whether I was hungry. I did not lie about whether I had eaten lunch. I ordered the salmon and I ate the whole thing and I sat across from him at the table and I felt like I was looking at him for the first time in a year.

He noticed. He did not say anything at the restaurant. But when we got in the car he put his hand on my hand and he said, "you came back tonight."

I cried in the passenger seat all the way home.

Week 2 the bloat dropped two pant sizes. Not from more weight loss. From standing-water bloat that finally drained.

Week 3 I let my husband hold me at night for the first time in 7 months. He fell asleep with his arm across my stomach and I lay there awake crying because the brick was gone and I had stopped believing it was ever going to leave.

Week 4 I told my book club the truth about what the last 14 months had actually been like. Three of the women at the table started crying. Two of them were on Wegovy. They had been lying to their husbands too.

Week 6 I started forgetting to take the gummies. Not because I was being careless. Because my body had stopped reminding me with the brick at the dinner table.

That is when I knew. The gummies were not papering over the problem. They had reset the stomach.

I have not lied to my husband about food, about the bathroom, or about how I feel in 47 days.

That number sounds small. Add up your own. Then tell me if it is small.

I am not a doctor and I am not telling you what to do with your body. What I can tell you is what worked for me after the kitchen sink approach failed for 11 months and the lies at the dinner table almost cost me my marriage.

If you are sitting at your own kitchen table right now and you have been telling your husband you ate dinner when you didn't, I hear you. I sat at that same table for 14 months telling the same lies to the man I have been married to for 38 years.

If you have stopped accepting dinner invitations because you cannot trust your stomach to make it through the meal, I hear you. I cancelled on my own daughter's birthday dinner in August and I told her it was a migraine. It wasn't a migraine.

If you have a bathroom shelf full of laxatives and probiotics and fiber blends that have not given you a single normal week in months, I hear you. I had $1,400 worth of bottles on my shelf and not one of them had ever been pointed at the right organ.

The reason none of it worked is the reason I told you about. Your slowed stomach is six feet upstream of every product that has ever been recommended to you. The Miralax, the Metamucil, the magnesium, the senna, every supplement, every doctor visit, every prescription, all of it has been aimed at a colon that was never the problem. The clog has been in the kitchen sink the whole time and you have been pouring drain cleaner into the bathtub.

Motilli is the only thing I have found that aims at the kitchen sink.

Two heart-shaped gummies every morning. Apigenin from standardized celery extract that wakes the smooth muscle in the stomach wall. Chlorophyllin in the stabilized form that deactivates the sulfur compounds the fermentation produces. The closest any of them came was a "no returns on opened bottles" sticker on the back of the box. Think about that for a second.
